---
title: "Quality assurance"
date-modified: "2026-05-12"
---

The use of alternative data sources in CPI compilation requires robust
quality assurance procedures. 

While many of the quality principles applied to traditional price
collection remain relevant, alternative data sources introduce new risks
that must be managed carefully. These risks may arise from the scale and
complexity of the datasets, the automated nature of processing
pipelines, and the reliance on systems and processes that are outside
the direct control of the National Statistical Office (NSO).

Quality assurance should therefore be embedded throughout the CPI
production process. Rather than being treated as a single stage of
validation, quality considerations should inform the assessment of
potential data sources, the design of processing systems, the
compilation of indices and the ongoing monitoring of outputs. Quality
assurance procedures should be proportionate to the scale and complexity
of the data source and should evolve as experience with the data
increases. NSOs are encouraged to develop quality assurance procedures
tailored to their own data sources, compilation methods and operational
environments.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Quality frameworks {#Qualityassurance-Qualityframeworks end="2121" data-start="1641"}

International statistical quality frameworks provide useful guidance for
structuring this work. The United Nations (UN) has published the *United
Nations National Quality Assurance Frameworks Manual for Official
Statistics ([UN NQAF
Manual](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/methodology/dataquality/))*, which
provides guidance on establishing quality frameworks within national
statistical systems. The manual includes specific guidance on quality
assurance for statistics compiled using administrative or other
non-statistical data sources.

Frameworks generally include a set of quality dimensions that can help
structure quality assurance activities. For example, the [Quality
Assurance Framework of the European Statistical
System](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/64157/4392716/ESS-QAF-V1-2final.pdf/bbf5970c-1adf-46c8-afc3-58ce177a0646)
identifies several principles relating to statistical outputs:

1.  *Relevance *- The degree to which the statistical product meets user
    needs in both coverage and content.
2.  *Accuracy & Reliability* - Accuracy is the proximity between an
    estimate and the unknown true value. Reliability is the closeness of
    early estimates to subsequent estimated values.
3.  *Timeliness and Punctuality* - Timeliness refers to the time gap
    between publication and the reference period. Punctuality refers to
    the gap between planned and actual publication dates.
4.  *Accessibility and Clarity* - Accessibility is the ease with which
    users are able to access the data, also reflecting the format in
    which the data are available and the availability of supporting
    information. Clarity refers to the quality and sufficiency of the
    metadata, illustrations and accompanying advice.
5.  *Comparability and Coherence* - Comparability is the degree to which
    data can be compared over time and domain. Coherence is the degree
    to which data that are derived from different sources or methods,
    but refer to the same topic, are similar.

With the advance of modern methods and systems, including the potential
use of machine learning and AI in the production of Official Statistics,
some other dimensions of quality are also being considered and proposed.
For example, reproducibility has been a key consideration in recent
years (see for example, [the Price Statistics Reproducibility
Project](https://un-task-team-for-scanner-data.github.io/reproducibility-project/docs/)),
while explainability and robustnesses have also been proposed in the
Machine Learning context (see [A Quality Concept for the Use of Machine
Learning in Official
Statistics](https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/ML2023_S2_Germany_Dumpert_Paper.pdf)). 

All quality dimensions remain applicable when using alternative data
sources for CPI production. In practice, however, their implementation
requires particular attention to both the characteristics of the data
source and the behaviour of the resulting statistical outputs. Quality
assurance activities can therefore be considered across several stages
of the CPI production process as described below. 

# Source assessment {#Qualityassurance-Sourceassessment end="3782" section-id="ncy3v2" data-start="3762"}

Before integrating a new data source into CPI compilation, NSOs should
evaluate whether it is suitable for statistical use. This assessment
should consider whether the data provide adequate coverage of the
products, outlets or market segments represented in the CPI, and whether
the concepts and definitions used in the data align with CPI
requirements.

Other important considerations include the stability of product
identifiers and classifications, the availability of metadata, and the
sustainability of access to the data source. Because alternative data
sources are often supplied by external organisations, changes in
provider systems, business practices or data delivery mechanisms may
affect the structure or interpretation of the data.

Exploratory analysis or pilot studies can be useful in assessing whether
the data source provides sufficient coverage, stability and quality for
CPI purposes.

Where alternative data are obtained from external providers, formal data
sharing agreements or contracts are typically required. These agreements
should specify the data schema, transfer frequency, delivery method and
responsibilities for maintaining the data supply. It is also good
practice to include provisions requiring advance notification of planned
changes to data structures, definitions or delivery processes so that
NSOs can make any necessary adjustments in advance. Where possible, any
validation checks carried out by the data supplier should be agreed and
documented.

More details of quality assurance at this stage of the process are
provided in the [Data selection and
acquisition](data-selection-and-acquisition.qmd) section. 

# Data ingestion and integrity checks {#Qualityassurance-Dataingestionandintegritychecks end="5318" section-id="5imlhi" data-start="5280"}

Once a data source has been established, quality assurance should begin
with checks on the integrity of incoming data deliveries. These checks
confirm that the data have been received as expected and that their
structure remains consistent over time.

Typical checks may include verifying the completeness of data
deliveries, confirming that key variables and identifiers are present
and correctly formatted, and monitoring the volume of observations
received. Sudden changes in data volumes, missing variables or
structural differences may indicate delivery errors or changes in
provider systems that require investigation.

At this stage it is often useful to
[standardise](standardising-the-data.qmd) incoming data into
a common internal schema used for CPI processing. For example, NSOs may
adopt consistent naming conventions and variable definitions for key
fields such as price, quantity, product identifiers or transaction
dates. [Standardising](standardising-the-data.qmd) the data
structure helps ensure consistency across different sources and
simplifies downstream processing.

Many NSOs implement automated validation pipelines or monitoring
dashboards to track incoming data deliveries and flag anomalies. These
tools can help detect missing data, structural changes or unusual shifts
in data volumes as soon as the data are ingested.

# Data preparation and processing {#Qualityassurance-Datapreparationandprocessing end="6649" section-id="94gjgs" data-start="6615"}

Quality assurance during data preparation focuses on ensuring that the
data have been correctly processed and classified for CPI use. This
stage often involves mapping products to the CPI classification,
identifying missing or duplicate observations, and detecting extreme or
implausible price movements. 

In the case of alternative data sources, particular attention may be
required to manage product identifiers, product relaunches or changes in
packaging and product characteristics. Because these datasets are
typically large and require automated processing pipelines,
reproducibility, documentation and version control are particularly
important.

The systems used to process alternative data sources should also be
appropriately tested and supported by the NSO's IT infrastructure.
Responsibilities for maintaining these systems, including the division
of roles between statistical production teams and IT departments, should
be clearly defined.

# Index compilation and validation {#Qualityassurance-Indexcompilationandvalidation end="7645" section-id="1l5dzyq" data-start="7610"}

After price indices have been compiled, quality assurance should focus
on the behaviour of the resulting statistical outputs. This may involve
analysing the volatility of indices, reviewing the contributions of
individual products or retailers, and comparing results with indices
produced using alternative methods or data sources.

Unexpected movements or structural breaks in the index may indicate
issues in the underlying data or processing procedures. For example,
changes in product coverage, filtering rules or matching algorithms may
affect index stability and should be investigated carefully.

Before introducing indices derived from alternative data sources into
live production, it is generally advisable to conduct impact analysis
comparing the results with existing CPI series (see section
on [Implementation](implementation.qmd)). Differences between
the new and existing approaches should be understood and documented, and
any methodological changes should be clearly explainable to users.

Some NSOs also use formal governance arrangements when introducing new
data sources or index methods, such as internal review panels or
external advisory groups (see as an example the UK\'s [advisory panels
for consumer prices - stakeholder and
technical](https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/the-authority-board/committees/national-statisticians-advisory-committees-and-panels/advisory-panels-for-consumer-price-statistics/)).
These structures can provide additional scrutiny and help ensure that
proposed methodological changes are robust and transparent.

# Ongoing monitoring {#Qualityassurance-Ongoingmonitoring end="8919" section-id="1vaoxy8" data-start="8898"}

The characteristics of alternative data sources may evolve over time as
retailers update systems, websites change structure, or consumer
purchasing behaviour shifts. Quality assurance should therefore include
ongoing monitoring of both the underlying data and the resulting
statistical outputs.

Monitoring activities may include tracking changes in product coverage,
retailer participation or identifier structures, reviewing the stability
of data deliveries, and periodically reassessing the representativeness
of the data source relative to the CPI universe.

Where automated or machine learning approaches are used in data
processing (for example in product classification or matching),
additional monitoring may be required to ensure that model performance
remains stable over time. Changes in product ranges or market behaviour
may affect the accuracy of such models and periodic review may therefore
be necessary. The section
on [classification ](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/spaces/GWGSD/pages/240910479/Classification)includes
a discussion on monitoring the accuracy of any machine learning models
used over time.
